title: The Birds and Beasts and the Carpenter

keywords: the birds and beasts and the carpenter
full_text:
In an ancient forest, the beasts of the field and the birds of the air held a council. A young lion, proud of his claws and majestic roar, asked the elder wolf what creature in the world was the most dangerous. The wolf shuddered and answered: 'Beware of the son of Adam! He possesses neither sharp fangs nor iron talons, yet by his craft and cunning, he traps the elephant in a pit, harnesses the ox to his plow, and cages the falcon in the sky.'

The young lion scoffed at this warning and set forth to conquer this mysterious creature. On the forest trail, he met a horse with an iron bit between its teeth. 'Who did this to you?' asked the lion. 'The son of Adam,' sighed the horse. Next, he met an ox with a ring in its nose and a heavy wooden yoke. 'The son of Adam has tamed me,' moaned the ox.

Continuing deeper into the woods, the lion encountered a slender man carrying an axe, an adze, and several heavy wooden planks upon his shoulder. 'Are you the son of Adam?' growled the lion. The carpenter bowed meekly: 'I am indeed a carpenter, a humble servant of Adam.'

The lion roared: 'Prepare to perish, for I am the king of the beasts!' The carpenter did not tremble. He said calmly: 'O king of the forest, slay me if you will, but first grant me leave to complete this wooden house I am building to shelter a noble beast from the coming winter tempests.'

Curious, the lion examined the sturdy wooden chest the carpenter was assembling. 'Is it large enough for a great monarch like me?' asked the lion. 'Test it yourself, sire,' invited the carpenter, holding open the sliding door.

The lion stepped inside the chest and curled his tail. Swiftly, the carpenter slid the heavy wooden lid into place, drove three iron nails through the latch, and smiled down through the air holes. The trapped lion roared in frustration, but the carpenter said: 'Learn, O beast, that brute strength is nothing before the patient craft of the mind.' Leaving the lion safely confined until he promised peace, the carpenter returned to his village.
moral: Human craft and intellect, when guided by prudence, can build shelters that tame the fiercest perils.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Birds and Beasts and the Carpenter"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
